notes: Edition composed by Claude from the collected headlines, reading titles and metadata only.
Each narrative is an idea that joins several different events; what it joins is listed at the top. It commits to a claim, and the last rung of every narrative is the case against it. Read both.
Where a narrative continues one from the previous edition it says what has changed since; every edition is kept, so the reader can step back to where we were.

Each narrative ends with 'How we got here': four horizons, since 2020, since 2008, since 1989 and since 1945, each the start of a regime the headlines are living inside, and sometimes a fifth that reaches further back and names its own starting year. They are a trajectory, not a verdict.

Each narrative sets one or two things to watch for: what should follow, by when, if its join is right. Later editions check them against their headlines; the ledger is data/watch.json and the count stands beside the narrative's firmness.

Each narrative looks ahead: the precedent its join most resembles, two or three paths with one favoured, and where the trajectory points over a decade. That is the writer's anticipation, drawn on what it knows of history and not only on the headlines; the expectations are the earliest dated signs of the favoured path, and are how the site checks it.
The connections are made by the model, not by the publishers. Follow any headline to the original report before repeating it.
Books and trajectories appear only where they change how a fragment or a horizon reads.

readings.line: The war's energy shock is now an order book for turbines, batteries and solar cells, and the factories making them are at capacity.

watch.what: A maker of gas turbines, transformers or grid batteries reports a record order backlog or longer delivery times and names energy security or the Gulf war.
watch.because: If the shock is turning into equipment purchases across many buyers at once, it will show first in the suppliers' order books rather than in any one country's fuel bill.

watch.what: A government in Asia, Africa or Latin America announces a solar, storage or nuclear tender and cites fuel import costs or the Hormuz closure.
watch.because: The join holds only if buyers who cannot change the fuel price are answering it with capital spending, and a tender naming the war is that answer in writing.

ahead.precedent: The closest case is 1973 to 1974, when the Arab oil embargo quadrupled the oil price and France answered with the Messmer plan of March 1974 to build dozens of nuclear reactors, Brazil launched its Proálcool ethanol programme in 1975 and Denmark began its turn to wind. Those programmes outlasted the high price, which collapsed in 1986. The difference now is that the buyers are mostly emerging economies and the main supplier of solar cells, batteries and much grid equipment is China, so the shock moves orders towards one country's factories.

paths.name: Orders outlast a peace deal
paths.text: Even if US-Iran talks reopen Hormuz in the coming months, contracts for turbines, storage and solar run for years, and ministries that have watched tankers burn will not cancel them. Expect more tenders citing energy security through the first half of next year and longer delivery times for turbines and transformers. The join points this way because the equipment is being bought by many unrelated buyers at once, not by one government reacting to one price.
paths.sign: A turbine or transformer maker reports a record backlog and says customers are waiting longer for delivery.

paths.name: Cheaper oil stalls the projects
paths.text: If a deal brings oil down sharply, as the 1986 collapse did, finance ministries may delay storage and solar tenders that were justified against expensive fuel. This is less likely than in the 1980s because solar and batteries are now cheaper than imported fuel at most prices seen this decade.
paths.sign: A government postpones or cancels a renewable or storage tender and cites lower oil prices.

paths.name: Shortages push grids back to diesel
paths.text: Turbine and transformer shortages could leave countries short of power and running old diesel and coal plants longer. It is unlikely to become the main story because solar and batteries can be installed in months where a gas turbine takes years.
paths.sign: A government extends the life of a coal or diesel plant and cites delays in equipment delivery.

ahead.decade: Over ten years the trajectory points to emerging economies depending less on imported fuel and more on imported equipment, much of it Chinese, so their exposure moves from the oil price to their trade relations with Beijing.

readings.claim: Iran says two tankers caught fire after hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz and Chile's SAAM reports lower earnings on fuel costs, while Siemens Energy says a Middle East power push is straining gas turbine supply, a Chinese solar cell line runs at full capacity, Adani Green turns to batteries for India's grid and an agency finds the energy crisis is speeding renewables in emerging economies. The fuel shock that began as a price is now being turned into purchases of power equipment. Governments and firms that cannot lower the price of imported fuel are buying the means to need less of it, and the factories that make that equipment are running near their limit.

events.label: Mines hit tankers, fuel costs cut earnings
Emerging economies grow and switch despite shock
Siemens Energy turbine supply strained
Chinese solar and reactor build
Indian storage and fuel blending
Households move power use to cheap hours

fragments.label: Hormuz and a Chilean shipper
fragments.text: La Tercera (Chile) reports Iran saying two oil tankers caught fire after hitting naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz. The same paper reports that SAAM, a Chilean port and towage company, earned less because of higher costs as fuel prices rose. The first is the cause in the strait; the second is what it does to a company's accounts on the other side of the world.

fragments.label: Cabo Verde and Karnataka
fragments.text: Channel Africa (South Africa) reports Cabo Verde's economy grew 7.6% despite the global energy shock, naming the shock as the condition against which growth is now measured. BusinessLine (India) reports Karnataka's charge that oil companies sold petrol with up to 31.2% ethanol, above the 20% limit. Blending more ethanol than allowed is one way to stretch imported fuel, though the headline does not say why the companies did it.

fragments.label: Turbines and batteries
fragments.text: Arab News (Saudi Arabia) reports Siemens Energy saying a push for power in the Middle East is straining the supply of gas turbines. The Economic Times (India) reports Adani Green turning to battery storage to deal with grid problems. Both are about the machines needed to generate and hold electricity, not about the fuel itself.

fragments.label: Chinese lines at full use
fragments.text: Yicai (China) reports a TOPCon solar cell project at 100% capacity use with a 95% yield, and the start of full construction on the nuclear island of what it calls the world's first commercial high-temperature gas-cooled reactor. Al Jazeera's Arabic site (Qatar) cites an agency finding that the energy crisis is speeding the move to renewables in emerging economies.

rungs.label: From fuel bill to capital spending

fragments.label: The shock changes form
fragments.text: Read together, these headlines show the energy shock in two forms. In the first it is a cost: a burning tanker, a shipping firm's lower earnings, petrol stretched with ethanol. In the second it is an order: turbines, batteries, solar cells and reactors. Buyers who cannot lower the price of imported oil and gas are spending on equipment that reduces how much of it they need, and the factories that make it are at or near their limit.

fragments.label: Households move their use
fragments.text: The same response appears at the scale of a kitchen. The Manila Times (Philippines) carries Beko's promotion of appliances that start when electricity is cheaper, and MARCA (Spain) publishes tomorrow's electricity price hour by hour. Where households cannot change the price, they change the hour at which they use power.

fragments.label: Separate cycles
fragments.text: Several of these stories have causes other than the war. Siemens Energy's turbine backlog had been building for years on data centres, desalination and population growth in the Gulf, and China's solar factories follow Chinese industrial policy and a price cycle that left the industry with too much capacity in recent years. Adani's grid problem is about transmission in India, and Cabo Verde's growth is mostly tourism. What these events do not share is a buyer answering the same price: some are buyers, some are sellers, and the sellers' order books might be full without any closed strait. The pattern may also come from business wires that publish company statements in English on a slow day.

horizons.label: Since 2020
horizons.text: The years since 2020 taught importers that fuel can be cut off by politics. Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 pushed the Dutch TTF gas price above 300 euros a megawatt-hour in August that year, and the EU answered with REPowerEU in May 2022, a plan to buy less Russian gas and install more solar. The US Inflation Reduction Act of August 2022 turned clean energy into industrial policy, with tax credits for factories at home. China meanwhile built so much solar and battery capacity that module prices fell by more than half between 2022 and 2024. The twelve-day Israel-Iran war of June 2025 and, by these headlines, the mining of Hormuz this year added the Gulf to the list of supplies that can stop. The result is a buyer who has learned twice in four years that imported fuel is a risk and that equipment is cheap, the condition in which the Al Jazeera report of emerging economies speeding their shift to renewables makes sense.

horizons.label: Since 2008
horizons.text: After 2008 China's stimulus and its five-year plans made solar panels, and later batteries, a national industry. The US imposed duties on Chinese panels from 2012 and the EU from 2013, but Chinese output kept growing and the cost of solar power fell by around 90 per cent over the decade. The Paris Agreement of December 2015 gave governments in poor and middle-income countries a reason to plan for renewables, and the falling price gave them the means. Gas turbines took a different path. A few Western and Japanese firms, Siemens, General Electric and Mitsubishi, kept that market, and after weak orders in the mid-2010s they cut jobs and capacity. That is why the Siemens Energy warning of strained turbine supply and the Yicai report of a solar line at full capacity describe two different industries: one concentrated in a handful of incumbents, the other built at scale in China in the years after the crash.

horizons.label: Since 1989
horizons.text: The decade after 1989 rebuilt electricity as a market. Britain privatised its power industry in 1990 and the 'dash for gas' followed, as combined-cycle gas turbines became the cheapest way to build a plant. EU directives from 1996 opened national grids to competition, and Spain's wholesale market, started in 1998, now sets the hourly price MARCA publishes each evening. India's reforms of 1991 and its Electricity Act of 2003 let private firms such as Adani build and sell power. Gas became the fuel of the liberalised grid because plants were quick to build and, in a world at peace, the fuel was cheap to import by pipeline and tanker. That bet depended on the long peace and on open sea lanes, the two things that the strikes on Ukraine's grid and the mines in Hormuz now put in doubt, and it is why a shortage of turbines matters to so many grids at once. The library holds no trajectory for this moment.

horizons.label: Since 1945
horizons.text: The postwar order ran on oil priced in dollars and shipped from the Gulf. Roosevelt's meeting with Ibn Saud in February 1945 set its terms, and newly independent states built their development plans on imported fuel. The Arab embargo of October 1973 showed what that meant for an importer, and the answers then resemble the answers in these headlines. Brazil launched Proálcool in 1975 to replace petrol with cane ethanol, the origin of the blending that Karnataka now accuses oil companies of overdoing. France chose nuclear in 1974, and the high-temperature gas-cooled reactor in the Yicai report descends from German pebble-bed designs of the 1960s. Daniel Yergin's The Prize describes the twentieth century as one in which control of fuel decided alliances. The headlines suggest that for importers the next phase will be decided by who makes the machines that replace it.

readings.line: Regulators now treat the recommendation system, not the single post, as the thing a platform must answer for.

watch.what: TikTok announces a change to its recommendation feed for European users, such as a non-personalised default or limits for minors, after the Commission's findings.
watch.because: If the design itself is now the regulated object, the remedy will be a change to the ranking system rather than the removal of particular videos.

watch.what: Britain, Australia, Brazil, India or Canada proposes or adopts rules on recommendation or addictive design features for minors.
watch.because: When several unrelated systems regulate the same object at once, other governments tend to copy the object, so the join predicts design rules rather than new content rules elsewhere.

ahead.precedent: The closest case is the American car in the 1960s. After Ralph Nader's Unsafe at Any Speed in 1965, Congress passed the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act in 1966, and regulation moved from blaming drivers to setting standards for the design of the car; manufacturers fought it and then complied within a decade. The difference now is that a feed is sold in every country at once, American courts treat ranking as protected speech in a way they never treated a steering column, and one of the regulators, China, uses the same tools for censorship.

paths.name: Europe forces design changes first
paths.text: The Commission's case under the Digital Services Act can end in a fine of up to 6% of global turnover or in commitments, and TikTok is likely to offer changes for EU users within months, as it withdrew its TikTok Lite rewards scheme in 2024 after Commission proceedings. California's law meanwhile stays tied up in court. The join points this way because the EU is the only regulator in the headlines with a design duty already in force against a named feature.
paths.sign: TikTok or the Commission announces commitments on the recommendation feed for EU users.

paths.name: US courts block the state laws
paths.text: Industry groups have won injunctions against several state laws on social media for minors on First Amendment grounds since 2023, and could win again in California, leaving Europe as the only large market with design rules. This is less likely to settle the matter because the new Congress may write its own rules.
paths.sign: A federal judge blocks California's law on addictive features while the case is heard.

paths.name: Congress passes a federal design law
paths.text: The new Democratic majority plans a wave of technology bills and could pass a children's online safety law that reaches feeds. With a president able to veto and Senate rules in place, a law within a year is unlikely.
paths.sign: The House passes a bill restricting algorithmic feeds for minors.

ahead.decade: Over ten years the trajectory points to recommendation systems being inspected and licensed like other consumer products in Europe and much of Asia, with the United States the main exception unless its courts change how they read ranking as speech.

readings.claim: The European Commission has accused TikTok of breaching EU rules through its content recommendation system, Google, Meta and TikTok are suing to block a California law restricting addictive social media features for children, and China's broadcasting regulator has opened a two-month campaign against vulgar and homogenised AI micro-dramas after removing 75,000 titles. In Brussels, California and Beijing the thing being regulated is the system that decides what a user is shown next, not a single post. That shift moves responsibility from the people who post to the companies that rank, and it is why the platforms are answering in court rather than by deleting content.

events.label: EU charges TikTok over recommendation system
Platforms sue over California addictive-features law
China's campaign against AI micro-drama sameness
Democrats prepare AI bills for Congress
Norwegian broadcaster explains social media habit

fragments.label: The EU and TikTok
fragments.text: Anadolu (Turkey) reports the EU accusing TikTok of violations in its content recommendation system, and NDR (Germany) reports the Commission targeting TikTok's 'pull effect'. franceinfo (France) lists TikTok in Brussels' sights among the day's main news. By these headlines the complaint is about how the app keeps users watching, not about any particular video.

fragments.label: California's law in court
fragments.text: International Business Times UK reports that Google, Meta and TikTok have sued to block a California law restricting addictive features for children. The companies are not defending a post; they are defending a design.

fragments.label: Beijing's micro-drama campaign
fragments.text: Sina (China) reports that the broadcasting regulator has started a two-month campaign against vulgar and homogenised AI micro-dramas, after 75,000 titles were removed earlier. The target is the volume and sameness of what the industry's systems produce and push, a problem of supply as much as of any one title.

fragments.label: Washington and Oslo
fragments.text: iefimerida (Greece), citing Reuters, reports that Democrats plan a flood of AI bills once they control Congress. NRK (Norway) runs an explainer on how everyone got hooked on social media. The first is a legislature that has passed little on platform design preparing to try; the second is a public broadcaster treating dependence on the feed as common knowledge.

fragments.label: From content to design
fragments.text: What joins these is the object of regulation. For two decades platform law in Europe and the US treated companies as hosts of other people's posts and asked them to remove illegal ones. The EU's case against TikTok and California's law instead treat the ranking system and the endless scroll as the product the company makes and answers for. China's campaign does the same from another direction, holding an industry responsible for what its systems mass-produce.

fragments.label: Why the answer is a lawsuit
fragments.text: When the post was the object, platforms could comply by deleting it. When the design is the object, compliance changes the business, because the recommendation system is what holds attention and so what sells advertising. That is why the platforms' response in California is a lawsuit and the Commission's language in Germany is about a 'pull effect'.

fragments.label: Different aims under one word
fragments.text: The three regulators want different things. The EU is enforcing duties on systemic risk under the Digital Services Act, California is protecting children from features it calls addictive, and China's regulator is policing taste and political safety in a fast-growing entertainment industry by removing titles, which is content control of the old kind. The Democrats' plans, by the headline, concern artificial intelligence in general, not feeds. What the events do not share is a purpose: calling all of them feed regulation puts a censor and a consumer-protection agency in one category, and only two of the cases are clearly about ranking design.

horizons.label: Since 2020
horizons.text: The years since 2020 made the feed the main way people passed time indoors. TikTok reached a billion monthly users in September 2021, a month before Frances Haugen's leak of Facebook research on Instagram and teenage girls. China issued rules on algorithmic recommendation in March 2022, among the first anywhere to require that users be able to switch personalised recommendations off. The EU adopted the Digital Services Act in October 2022 and applied it to the largest platforms in August 2023, with duties to assess the risks their systems create; the case NDR reports against TikTok's 'pull effect' is that law in use. In the US the Surgeon General warned about social media and young people in 2023, states passed design laws for minors, and Australia legislated an under-16 ban in November 2024. The generative wave after ChatGPT then added machine-made content to the feed, which is what Beijing's campaign against AI micro-dramas now addresses.

horizons.label: Since 2008
horizons.text: The iPhone of 2007 and the app stores that followed put a feed in every pocket. Facebook moved its News Feed towards algorithmic ranking around 2009, Instagram launched in 2010 and switched to ranking in 2016, and ByteDance launched Douyin in China in 2016 and TikTok abroad a year later, built on recommendation rather than on following friends. Advertising paid for all of it, so time spent became the measure of success. Shoshana Zuboff's The Age of Surveillance Capitalism, published in 2019, described the business as one that predicts and shapes behaviour for sale. The Cambridge Analytica scandal and the EU's General Data Protection Regulation, both in 2018, fixed regulators' attention on data. The California law the platforms are now suing over moves the question from what data is collected to what the collected data is used to make users do. The library holds no trajectory for this turn.

horizons.label: Since 1989
horizons.text: The legal frame these cases are breaking was set in the 1990s. The web was opened to the public in 1991, and Netscape's listing in August 1995 told investors it was a business. In 1996 Section 230 of the US Communications Decency Act said an online service would not be treated as the publisher of what its users post, and the EU's e-Commerce Directive of 2000 gave hosts a similar shield if they removed illegal content once told. Both laws imagined a bulletin board, not a ranking engine, and for twenty years regulation argued about takedowns. The EU's charge against TikTok's recommendation system and California's addictive-features law are attempts to reach the part those laws left out: the company's own choice of what appears next. The platforms' lawsuit argues that this choice is itself protected speech, an argument the 1996 frame made available.

horizons.label: Since 1945
horizons.text: Before the feed there was the schedule, and after 1945 most states treated what a mass audience was shown as a public matter. Britain kept television as a BBC monopoly until ITV began in 1955, under rules written by Parliament. The US Federal Communications Commission adopted the Fairness Doctrine in 1949. The People's Republic placed broadcasting under the state from 1949, the line that runs to the regulator now campaigning against AI micro-dramas. Sweden banned television advertising aimed at children under twelve in 1991, an early rule aimed at an audience rather than at a single programme. Marshall McLuhan argued in Understanding Media in 1964 that the form of a medium matters more than its content. The Commission and California now act on something like that idea, treating the form of the feed, not its items, as what must be regulated. The library holds no trajectory for postwar broadcasting law.

readings.line: A failed bank or state fund turns into a case against the presidents and judges near it, and its fines divide governments for years.

watch.what: A minister, central bank official or financial regulator in Paraguay or Brazil resigns or is dismissed over the Ueno or Banco Master cases.
watch.because: If the shape holds, a bank's records move upwards from bankers to the officials who supervised or ruled on it, in both countries rather than only one.

watch.what: UMNO pays Najib's RM50 million fine and he goes home, and Loke or another DAP minister leaves the government.
watch.because: The join says the cost of a fund's collapse ends up borne by people in office years later, so the fine should be paid in political posts as well as money.

ahead.precedent: The closest case is Iceland after its three banks failed in October 2008: former prime minister Geir Haarde was tried before the special Landsdómur court in 2012, the first such trial in its history, and convicted on one minor count without penalty. Malaysia's own 1MDB case is the other: revealed in 2015, it helped end Barisan Nasional's rule in the 2018 election and put Najib in prison in 2022. The present differs because Paraguay's president is still in office and his Colorado Party holds Congress, and because in Brazil the official named is a judge of the court that will rule on the case.

paths.name: Peña survives, ministers fall
paths.text: Impeachment in Paraguay needs two-thirds of the Chamber of Deputies to charge and two-thirds of the Senate to remove, and the Colorado Party holds majorities in both. Peña is more likely to survive while ministers or bank supervisors resign within weeks, and the Itaipu tariff review slips into next year. The join points this way because in each case the record reaches officials, but only those without their own votes lose office.
paths.sign: Paraguay's finance minister or central bank president resigns over the Ueno crisis.

paths.name: Paraguay removes its president
paths.text: Paraguay's Congress removed Fernando Lugo in June 2012 in about a day and a half, so speed is not the obstacle; votes are. If enough Colorado deputies decide Peña is a liability, Vice-President Pedro Alliana takes over before the new year.
paths.sign: The Chamber of Deputies votes to send impeachment charges against Peña to the Senate.

paths.name: The cases settle into inquiries
paths.text: The cases could become long investigations with no resignations, as many Latin American bank cases did in the 2000s. This is unlikely because impeachment is already formally under way in Paraguay and a plea deal in the Master case means a witness is talking.
paths.sign: Paraguay's Congress shelves the impeachment proceedings without a vote.

ahead.decade: Over ten years the trajectory points to bank supervision becoming a political office in its own right in Latin America and Southeast Asia, with each large failure tested in congresses and courts rather than closed by regulators.

readings.claim: Paraguay's Congress has resumed impeachment proceedings against President Santiago Peña as the Ueno bank crisis deepens, threatening to delay the review of the Itaipu dam tariff with Brazil; in Brazil, Daniel Vorcaro's phone records 316 interactions with Supreme Court justice Alexandre de Moraes and a plea deal in the Banco Master case has been approved; Chile's Supreme Court has upheld a large fine on the former chief executive of Primus Capital; and in Malaysia, Najib Razak's return home has stalled while UMNO moves to pay his RM50 million fine, which Anwar Ibrahim says he disagrees with and a coalition minister says will cost his resignation. In each case a failed bank or fund has become a question about the people who governed, judged or protected it. The losses are financial, but what is being decided is who in office answers for a collapse, and who pays.

events.label: Ueno bank crisis and Peña impeachment
Banco Master records reach Supreme Court justice
Chile upholds fine on Primus ex-CEO
Najib's fine splits Malaysia's coalition

fragments.label: Ueno and Peña
fragments.text: Al Jazeera (Qatar) reports Paraguay resuming impeachment proceedings against President Peña as a financial crisis deepens, and Estado de Minas (Brazil) calls it a political earthquake after the Ueno bank crisis. O Globo (Brazil) reports that the crisis threatens to delay the review of the Itaipu tariff, the price at which the two countries share the dam's power. A bank's failure has moved to the presidency and to a treaty. The Spanish and Portuguese Wikipedias' most-viewed pages were Peña, the Colorado Party and Ueno Bank.

fragments.label: Master and Moraes
fragments.text: Estado de Minas reports that Daniel Vorcaro's phone records 316 interactions with Supreme Court justice Alexandre de Moraes in the months before Vorcaro's arrest. O Globo reports that Justice Edson Fachin approved the plea agreement of the former owner of Reag in the Master case. The inquiry that began with a bank now reaches the court that oversees it.

fragments.label: Primus in Chile
fragments.text: La Tercera (Chile) reports the Supreme Court upholding a large fine by the market regulator, the CMF, against the former chief executive of Primus Capital. Here the collapse has gone through regulator and court and ended with one executive paying.

fragments.label: Najib's fine
fragments.text: Al Jazeera's Arabic site asks why Najib Razak's return home stalled when he was about to leave prison. The Star (Malaysia) reports Prime Minister Anwar disagreeing with UMNO paying Najib's RM50 million fine while calling it the party's prerogative, and Loke saying his resignation takes effect the moment Najib gets home. Years after money left a state investment fund, the fine is still dividing a government.

fragments.label: The same question
fragments.text: In all four places the question being decided is who in public life answers for a financial collapse. In Paraguay it is the president; in Brazil a Supreme Court justice whose contacts with a banker are now in the record; in Chile an executive, through a regulator's fine; in Malaysia a former prime minister and the party that wants to pay his fine for him. A bank's records, phones and fines have become political evidence, and whether an official is protected depends on who holds the votes.

fragments.label: Chile as the contrast
fragments.text: Chile is the case where the system ran its course without reaching government: a regulator fined, a court upheld, an executive paid. Paraguay and Brazil show what happens when a bank's contacts run to the people who would normally do the judging, and Malaysia shows that the cost can still be collected from a coalition years after the conviction.

fragments.label: Four kinds of event
fragments.text: These are four different kinds of event. Ueno is a bank failure now in the hands of Paraguay's Congress; Banco Master is a fraud inquiry in which a justice's contacts have been reported, not charged; Primus is a closed regulatory case; and Najib's fine is the tail of a 2020 conviction, now about coalition politics and a pardons board rather than any bank. What they do not share is a cause: no single rate rise, regulator or lender lies behind them, and Latin American bank scandals have reached presidents since the 1990s. The join may describe the ordinary politics of countries with concentrated banking, noticed because Brazilian and Chilean papers covered their region on the same day.

horizons.label: Since 2020
horizons.text: The banks failing now grew in the years of cheap money and then met dear money. Pandemic credit in 2020 and 2021 was followed by the fastest rate rises in decades: Brazil's central bank took its Selic rate from 2% in March 2021 to 13.75% by August 2022. Banks that had grown by promising savers high returns, as Banco Master was reported to have done before its liquidation in 2025, found the gap between what they paid and what they earned hard to close. The failures of Silicon Valley Bank and Credit Suisse in March 2023 showed that deposits can leave in a day once a phone can move them. In Malaysia the same years produced the politics behind The Star's headlines: Najib convicted in July 2020, jailed in August 2022, his sentence and fine halved by the Pardons Board in February 2024, and UMNO now inside Anwar's coalition, which is why paying his RM50 million fine divides the government. The library holds no trajectory for these years of rates and pardons.

horizons.label: Since 2008
horizons.text: The 2008 crisis established that bank failures could be tried as politics. Lehman's collapse in September 2008 was followed in Iceland by the trial of a former prime minister before a special court in 2012, and across Europe by inquiries into who had let the banks grow. Adam Tooze's Crashed describes how the rescue itself became the political issue of the decade. In Brazil the shape came through prosecutors and judges: the Lava Jato inquiry from 2014 used plea deals to move from a money changer to the state oil company to presidents, and made the Supreme Court a central political actor. Alexandre de Moraes, appointed in 2017, became its most powerful judge through the inquiries into disinformation and the coup plot. That is why Vorcaro's 316 interactions with Moraes, and Fachin's approval of a plea deal, are read as political news, and why 1MDB, founded in 2009, was the same decade's Asian case.

horizons.label: Since 1989
horizons.text: Paraguay's present politics begin in February 1989, when General Alfredo Stroessner was overthrown after thirty-five years, but his Colorado Party kept power through elections and has lost the presidency only once since, to Fernando Lugo in 2008. Financial liberalisation in the 1990s brought Paraguayan bank crises in 1995 and again in 1997 and 1998, each handled by a party that also ran the state. In Malaysia the Asian crisis of 1997 split Prime Minister Mahathir from his deputy, Anwar Ibrahim, who was sacked and jailed in 1998; the same Anwar is now prime minister, saying what he thinks of UMNO paying Najib's fine. Chile's market regulator, reorganised as the CMF in 2017, descends from supervision built after Chile's bank collapse of 1982. These countries learned in the 1990s that a liberalised bank needs a supervisor independent of the ruling party, and the Ueno and Master cases test whether that lesson held. The library holds no trajectory for these crises.

horizons.label: Since 1945
horizons.text: The Itaipu headline reaches back to the Cold War. Brazil's military government, in power since the coup of March 1964, signed the Itaipu Treaty with Stroessner's Paraguay in April 1973 to build what became the largest dam in the world on their shared river. Each country owns half the power, but Paraguay uses little of its share and sells the rest to Brazil on terms set in the treaty's Annex C, which was due for review fifty years on, in 2023. For Paraguay the tariff is a large part of state revenue and a question of sovereignty; for Brazil it is part of the price of electricity in its industrial south. The postwar habit of a large state and a small neighbour bargaining through two dictatorships left a treaty that now has to be renegotiated by a president facing impeachment, which is why O Globo reports a bank crisis in Asunción as a Brazilian energy story.

readings.line: Homes in growing cities are now priced by money earned elsewhere, so a rise in local wages no longer buys a place to live.

watch.what: Portugal's government announces a new tax, limit or rule on home purchases by non-residents or foreign buyers.
watch.because: If outside money setting the price is the mechanism, governments will move from local supply rules to acting on the buyer, which none of the responses in these headlines yet does.

watch.what: A second government in Europe or Australasia publishes the share of home purchases made by foreign or non-resident buyers, or proposes curbing them.
watch.because: The join claims the mismatch between local wages and outside buyers is common to several countries, so it should surface as a counted figure or a proposal beyond Portugal.

ahead.precedent: The closest case is Vancouver in 2016, when British Columbia imposed a 15% tax on foreign buyers in August after prices had risen about 30% in a year; sales fell for a few months, prices rose again in 2017, and Canada banned most foreign purchases of homes from January 2023. New Zealand banned most foreign buyers in 2018, and Australia stopped foreign purchases of established homes from April 2025. Portugal differs because it sends emigrants out as well as drawing buyers in, so the people priced out leave the country, not only the city.

paths.name: Taxes on outside buyers spread
paths.text: Within a year Portugal and other southern European governments move from tenders and zoning to taxes or limits on non-resident buyers, following Canada, New Zealand and Australia; Spain's January 2025 proposal of a tax of up to 100% on non-EU non-resident buyers is the template. Prices slow but do not fall. The join points this way because local supply measures leave the price-setting buyer untouched, and record prices alongside mass emigration make that visible.
paths.sign: A southern European government includes a tax or limit on non-resident buyers in its budget or housing plan.

paths.name: Supply and subsidy only
paths.text: Governments keep to tenders, zoning changes and payments, as in Alentejo and Medellín, because foreign buyers bring tax and tourism revenue. Prices keep rising and emigration of the young continues.
paths.sign: A housing package is announced with new building subsidies and no rule on who may buy.

paths.name: High rates bring prices down
paths.text: With central banks holding rates high against the war's oil price, house prices could fall, as after 2008. This is unlikely where foreign buyers pay cash and do not borrow locally.
paths.sign: Portugal's statistics institute reports a quarterly fall in house prices.

ahead.decade: Over ten years the trajectory points to housing being governed as a border question, with more countries treating who may buy a home as they treat who may work, while emigration from expensive southern European countries continues.

readings.claim: Foreign buyers made 16% of home purchases in Portugal as prices hit records, while 780,000 people left the country in five years; two Brazilian firms are raising up to R$400 million from Brazilians to build and renovate homes in the United States; essential workers in Australia cannot afford rents; Pablo Iglesias says a higher minimum wage only works with intervention in housing; and Canada funds homelessness programmes, Spain makes regions report every housing payment, and Medellín and Comox rewrite their zoning. These events share a mechanism: homes in places people want to live are priced by money earned somewhere else, while the people who work there are paid local wages. Governments answer with local rules, and the price is set beyond their reach.

events.label: Portugal sells homes abroad as residents leave
Brazilian savers fund US home building
Australian essential workers priced out of rents
Spanish and French arguments over wages and housing
Homelessness funding and Berlin's cold
Local zoning and tenders in three places

fragments.label: Portugal's two numbers
fragments.text: SAPO (Portugal) reports foreigners made 16% of home purchases while prices reached record highs. Observador (Portugal) reports 780,000 people left Portugal in the last five years. The Times of India runs a feature on Cristiano Ronaldo's record $7 million Lisbon apartment, bought in 2018. In one day's headlines the same country is selling homes to people from abroad and losing its own residents abroad.

fragments.label: Brazilian savings, American homes
fragments.text: O Globo (Brazil) reports two firms, Leste and EQI, seeking up to R$400 million from Brazilian investors to finance building and renovating homes in the US. Here the money runs the other way: savers in a middle-income country fund housing in a rich one because the return is there.

fragments.label: Workers and the homeless
fragments.text: ABC (Australia) asks why essential workers cannot afford the rental market. taz (Germany) reports on homelessness in Berlin as the nights get dark and cold. CBC (Canada) reports Quebec's government panning the federal budget while mayors praise its funding to fight homelessness.

fragments.label: Wages and local rules
fragments.text: In MARCA (Spain) Pablo Iglesias argues that raising the minimum wage works only if the state also intervenes in the housing market, and El Mundo reports the government will require regions to report every housing-related payment. Sud Ouest (France) calls housing a crack in the republican pact. El Colombiano reports Medellín's new land-use plan rewriting housing rules, CBC reports Comox council downzoning a proposed condo site, and Observador reports Alentejo's EU-funded programme opening 46.1 million euros in housing tenders.

fragments.label: Where the price is set
fragments.text: What joins these is that the price of a home and the wage of the person who needs it are set in different places. Portugal's record prices are bid partly by buyers whose income is earned abroad, the Brazilian fund seeks returns from American homes, and Ronaldo's flat was bought with a footballer's international earnings. The essential worker in Australia and the minimum-wage earner Iglesias describes are paid in the local labour market, which is why a wage rise alone does not reach the rent.

fragments.label: What governments can reach
fragments.text: The responses in the headlines are all local: zoning in Medellín and Comox, tenders in Alentejo, reporting rules in Spain, homelessness funds in Canada. None of them acts on where the buying money comes from. Portugal's emigration figure suggests what happens instead: those who cannot meet the price leave, which ends the mismatch in a way no ministry chose.

fragments.label: Mostly domestic pressure
fragments.text: Most of the price pressure in these places is domestic. Australian rents follow population growth, interest rates and slow building; Berlin's homelessness has many causes; and 84% of Portuguese purchases are still made by residents. The 780,000 who left Portugal mostly left for higher wages, not lower rents, and the Brazilian fund is a small product while Ronaldo's flat is an eight-year-old celebrity purchase. What the events do not share is a buyer: only in Portugal does a headline name foreign buyers, and Comox's downzoning is a council choosing fewer homes, a local decision that has nothing to do with outside money.

horizons.label: Since 2020
horizons.text: The pandemic made it possible to earn a foreign salary while living in Lisbon. Portugal introduced a digital nomad visa in October 2022, while its non-habitual resident regime, which offered low tax to foreigners who moved there, was closed to new applicants from 2024. The golden visa route through property purchase was ended in October 2023 under the Mais Habitação package, and Spain ended its own in April 2025, but foreign buying continued, as SAPO's 16% shows. Interest rates then rose: the European Central Bank from July 2022 and the Reserve Bank of Australia from May 2022, which made borrowing dearer for local buyers while cash buyers from abroad were less affected. Rents in Australian cities rose sharply in 2022 and 2023 as migration resumed after the borders reopened, the condition behind ABC's question about essential workers. The library holds no trajectory for these visa and rate changes.

horizons.label: Since 2008
horizons.text: Portugal's two numbers come out of the crisis that followed 2008. In May 2011 the country took a 78 billion euro bailout from the EU and the IMF, cut wages and pensions, and lost a generation to emigration, with around 100,000 people a year leaving in the worst years. To bring money in, governments created the non-habitual resident regime in 2009 and the golden visa in 2012, and Airbnb, founded in 2008, turned old Lisbon flats into short lets. Prices recovered and then rose past their pre-crisis level. In Spain the same years produced the indignados in Madrid's Puerta del Sol in May 2011, then Podemos, then Pablo Iglesias as deputy prime minister in 2020. His argument in MARCA that a minimum wage rise fails without intervention in housing is a lesson from that path, in which the movement reached government and rents kept rising.

horizons.label: Since 1989
horizons.text: The free movement of money that lets a foreigner buy a flat in Lisbon was written into European law around 1989. The EU's capital movements directive of 1988 took effect for most members in July 1990, and the Maastricht Treaty extended free capital movement to the rest of the world from 1994. The euro in 1999 then gave Portugal and Spain German interest rates and a credit boom, and Spain built homes faster than any other large European country until 2007. The same years made some earnings international. The Bosman ruling of December 1995 let footballers move freely between European clubs, and the global market for players that followed paid for the $7 million Lisbon apartment the Times of India describes Cristiano Ronaldo buying in 2018. A Portuguese nurse and a Portuguese footballer now bid for homes in the same city with incomes set in different markets.

horizons.label: Since 1945
horizons.text: After 1945 western Europe treated housing as part of the welfare state. France built its HLM estates, West Germany its social housing, and public companies came to own much of Berlin; the republican pact Sud Ouest says is cracking is that settlement. Portugal stood outside it. Under Salazar's dictatorship around a million Portuguese emigrated in the 1960s, many to the shanty towns around Paris. After the Carnation Revolution of April 1974, the constitution of 1976 wrote a right to housing into Article 65. Tony Judt's Postwar describes how the postwar state promised a home as well as work. The present reverses that for Portugal: it again loses its young abroad, this time to cities where they can earn more, while its homes are bought by foreigners, and the constitutional right is pursued through EU-funded tenders such as Alentejo's 46.1 million euros.
